title: Chapter 11 Drill: Thoracic, Pediatric, Genitourinary, Gynecologic, and Neurosurgical Topics

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman with breast cancer reports back pain for two weeks, then new leg weakness and urinary retention. MRI shows epidural compression of the thoracic spinal cord by a vertebral metastasis. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Oral analgesics and outpatient imaging follow-up
Lumbar puncture to relieve spinal pressure, followed by chemotherapy, bed rest, and physical therapy at home for a month
High-dose dexamethasone and urgent surgical decompression or radiation, according to stability and prognosis
Chemotherapy alone with bed rest for a month
items.explanation: Malignant epidural spinal cord compression is an oncologic emergency, and function depends on speed. High-dose corticosteroids are started, then surgery for instability or a single level of compression, and radiation for radiosensitive tumors or poor surgical candidates. Delay causes permanent paralysis. Lumbar puncture can worsen the compression, and chemotherapy alone is too slow to reverse deficits.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man has been unable to void for 12 hours, with suprapubic pain and a palpable bladder. A urinary catheter is placed easily and drains 1,100 mL. What complication should be monitored for after decompression?
options: Postobstructive diuresis with fluid and electrolyte loss
Immediate bladder rupture from sudden emptying
Hypernatremia from retained free water
Acute severe hypertension from catecholamine release
items.explanation: Relief of chronic or high-volume obstruction can trigger postobstructive diuresis, so urine output, volume status, and electrolytes need monitoring and replacement when necessary. Rupture from emptying does not occur. Sodium loss and water loss make hypovolemia and low potassium or magnesium more likely than free-water retention. Hypertension from decompression is not a recognized pattern; hypotension from volume loss is.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has fever, lower abdominal pain, and cervical motion tenderness. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 6 cm complex right adnexal mass consistent with a tubo-ovarian abscess. She is stable and tolerating fluids. What is the initial treatment?
options: Immediate total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, with image-guided drainage if no improvement within days
Oral analgesics alone and repeat imaging in a month
A single dose of intramuscular antibiotic and discharge
items.explanation: A tubo-ovarian abscess from pelvic inflammatory disease is first treated with broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics, with percutaneous or surgical drainage if she fails to improve within about 48 to 72 hours or if the abscess ruptures. Hysterectomy is for rupture with sepsis or failure of all other care. Analgesics alone allow progression. A single dose is outpatient treatment for uncomplicated cervicitis, not an abscess.

items.stem: A 2-month-old infant has persistent jaundice with direct hyperbilirubinemia, pale clay-colored stools, and dark urine. Ultrasound shows an absent or contracted gallbladder. Which management gives the best outcome in this condition?
options: Observation for another three months to see whether stools turn normal
Cholecystectomy with common duct exploration and stenting
Hepatoportoenterostomy (Kasai procedure), ideally within the first two months of life
Phototherapy and discontinuation of breastfeeding
items.explanation: Cholestasis with acholic stools suggests biliary atresia, and the outcome depends on early drainage by hepatoportoenterostomy, with better bile flow when done before about two months. Waiting loses native liver function and leads toward transplant. Cholecystectomy does not treat intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct obliteration. Phototherapy treats unconjugated bilirubin, and breastfeeding does not cause direct hyperbilirubinemia.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man has dyspnea, drooping of the eyelids that worsens by evening, and a 6 cm anterior mediastinal mass on CT. Antibody testing for acetylcholine receptor is positive. What is the best treatment of the mass?
options: Needle biopsy and chemotherapy as the only treatment, leaving the thymus and the mass in place
Complete thymectomy, ideally after medical optimization of the myasthenia
Mediastinoscopy with observation of the mass
Radiation alone to avoid anesthetic risk
items.explanation: A mediastinal mass with myasthenia gravis suggests thymoma, and the preferred treatment is complete resection of the thymus and tumor, with preoperative optimization of neuromuscular function. Thymoma is assessed for invasion, and chemotherapy and radiation are adjuncts for advanced disease. Biopsy with drugs alone and radiation alone sacrifice the best local control, and observation leaves a potentially invasive tumor in place.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with severe low back pain develops saddle numbness, urinary retention with overflow incontinence, and weakness in both legs over six hours. MRI shows a massive central disc herniation at L4 to L5. What is the appropriate management?
options: Emergency surgical decompression
Physical therapy with outpatient follow-up
Epidural steroid injection in the clinic next week
Bed rest for several weeks with analgesics
items.explanation: Cauda equina syndrome presents with saddle anesthesia, bladder and bowel dysfunction, and bilateral leg weakness, and it requires emergency decompression to prevent permanent loss of sphincter and motor function, ideally within hours. Therapy, injections, and rest are treatments for ordinary radiculopathy and delay the operation. Outcomes worsen steadily as time passes after the onset of retention.

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy has a painless, smooth abdominal mass that crosses neither the midline nor the spine. He is hypertensive, and urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria. Imaging shows an intrarenal solid mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Neuroblastoma, a tumor that classically crosses the midline and encases vessels
Hepatoblastoma, a tumor with elevated alpha-fetoprotein
Polycystic kidney disease, a bilateral cystic condition
Wilms tumor, a kidney tumor that is treated with nephrectomy and chemotherapy
items.explanation: A smooth flank mass with hypertension and an intrarenal lesion in a young child points to Wilms tumor, treated by nephrectomy with staged chemotherapy, and the contralateral kidney is assessed. Neuroblastoma is typically extrarenal, calcified, and crosses the midline. Hepatoblastoma is hepatic with high alpha-fetoprotein. Polycystic disease is bilateral and cystic, not a solitary solid mass.

items.stem: A 5-week-old boy has projectile nonbilious vomiting after each feed and remains hungry. Examination shows visible gastric peristalsis. Laboratory values show a low chloride and a high bicarbonate. What should be done before surgery?
options: Proceed directly to pyloromyotomy to relieve the obstruction, since the electrolyte values will normalize afterward on their own
Give sodium bicarbonate to treat the low chloride
Correct dehydration and the hypochloremic alkalosis with isotonic saline containing dextrose and potassium
Begin a trial of oral feeding with an acid-suppressing drug
items.explanation: Pyloric stenosis causes loss of gastric acid and chloride, giving a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Surgery is not an emergency, and operating before correction risks postoperative apnea from the alkalosis. Resuscitation uses isotonic saline with dextrose, and potassium once urine is flowing. Bicarbonate worsens alkalosis. Feeding trials do not relieve the muscular obstruction, which needs pyloromyotomy afterward.

items.stem: A newborn has copious oral secretions, choking with the first feeding, and cyanosis. A feeding tube cannot be passed beyond 10 cm, and the abdomen is gas filled on radiography. What is the most likely anomaly?
options: Isolated esophageal atresia without a fistula
Esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula
H-type tracheoesophageal fistula without atresia
Congenital duodenal atresia with a double bubble
items.explanation: A blind proximal pouch causes drooling and choking, and a distal fistula to the trachea lets air enter the stomach, so the abdomen is gas filled. This is the most common variant. Pure atresia gives a gasless abdomen. An H-type fistula allows tube passage and presents later with cough on feeding. Duodenal atresia presents with bilious vomiting and a double bubble, not with failure to pass a tube.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with painless gross hematuria. He has a long smoking history and no pain, fever, or trauma. What is the most appropriate workup?
options: Cystoscopy and upper tract imaging with CT urography
Urine culture and treatment for a presumed urinary infection
Observation because painless bleeding is usually benign
Renal ultrasound only without lower tract evaluation
items.explanation: Painless gross hematuria in an older smoker is bladder cancer until shown otherwise, and evaluation requires cystoscopy plus imaging of the upper tract. A culture alone is insufficient when no infection is evident. Observation is inappropriate because the risk of malignancy is high. Ultrasound alone misses urothelial and small bladder tumors and does not examine the bladder mucosa.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man has sudden left flank pain radiating to the groin with hematuria. CT shows a 4 mm stone in the distal ureter, mild hydronephrosis, normal temperature, and normal creatinine. What is the best initial management?
options: Immediate nephrostomy tube placement
Analgesia and medical expulsive therapy with an alpha-blocker, with return precautions
Open ureterolithotomy under general anesthesia, since the stone is obstructing and causing hydronephrosis
Intravenous antibiotics for ten days with no analgesics
items.explanation: Small distal ureteral stones, especially those of 5 mm or less, commonly pass spontaneously, and analgesia with an alpha-blocker aids passage in selected patients. Nephrostomy or stenting is reserved for infection above an obstruction, a solitary kidney, or intractable pain. Open surgery is obsolete for this stone. Antibiotics are not needed without infection, and analgesia should be given.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has sudden severe right lower abdominal pain with vomiting. Ultrasound shows an enlarged right ovary of 7 cm with a 6 cm cyst, and Doppler flow is present. What is the correct management?
options: Oophorectomy for every dusky ovary, because a dark appearance proves the ovary is nonviable
Observation because normal Doppler flow excludes torsion
Immediate hysterectomy and oophorectomy
Laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation, even if the ovary appears dusky
items.explanation: Ovarian torsion is a clinical diagnosis, and preserved Doppler flow does not exclude it, since the ovary has dual blood supply. Laparoscopic detorsion often restores function even in a dark ovary, so conservation is advised in young women, with cystectomy afterward when appropriate. Removal of a dusky ovary is no longer the rule. Hysterectomy has no place in this setting.

items.stem: A 3-day-old term infant has bilious vomiting and a soft abdomen. The upper gastrointestinal contrast study shows the duodenojejunal junction to the right of the spine with a corkscrew duodenum. What is the best management?
options: Observation and a repeat contrast study in a week, since the infant is hemodynamically stable and has a soft abdomen
Rectal biopsy to exclude absent ganglion cells
Emergency Ladd procedure because of the risk of midgut volvulus and bowel loss
Pyloromyotomy through a supraumbilical incision
items.explanation: Bilious emesis in a newborn is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise, and an abnormally placed duodenojejunal junction confirms it. Delay risks infarction of the midgut, so surgery proceeds as an emergency using the Ladd procedure, dividing bands, widening the mesentery, and placing the bowel in a nonrotated position. Rectal biopsy addresses Hirschsprung disease, and pyloromyotomy treats nonbilious vomiting.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt has two days of headache, vomiting, and drowsiness. Examination shows upward gaze limitation and a bulging fontanelle-equivalent tension in the scalp. The shunt reservoir does not refill. What is the most likely cause?
options: Shunt obstruction causing recurrent hydrocephalus
Viral gastroenteritis unrelated to the shunt
Migraine with associated vomiting
Normal pressure hydrocephalus from aging
items.explanation: Headache, vomiting, lethargy, and a sunsetting gaze in a shunted child point to raised intracranial pressure from shunt failure, most often proximal catheter obstruction, and a reservoir that does not refill supports it. Imaging and urgent neurosurgical revision follow. Gastroenteritis and migraine would not explain the gaze palsy and drowsiness, and normal pressure hydrocephalus is a disorder of older adults.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has a stab wound to the upper arm, with inability to extend the wrist and fingers and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand. The wound is clean and bleeding is controlled. Which nerve is most likely injured?
options: The median nerve, which gives thumb opposition
The ulnar nerve, which gives finger abduction and adduction
The musculocutaneous nerve, which gives elbow flexion
The radial nerve, which gives wrist and finger extension
items.explanation: Wrist drop with loss of finger extension and sensation to the dorsum of the hand is radial nerve injury, as in humeral shaft trauma or arm wounds. Median nerve loss gives weak thumb opposition and a hand of benediction. Ulnar loss causes clawing and weak finger spread. Musculocutaneous injury weakens elbow flexion and causes lateral forearm sensory loss, so wrist extension is spared.

items.stem: A 62-year-old retired electrician has a 2.5 cm spiculated nodule in the right upper lobe on chest CT, avid on PET scan, with no enlarged mediastinal nodes and negative brain imaging. Pulmonary function testing is acceptable. What is the best next step?
options: Repeat chest CT in three months because the lesion is under 3 cm and a surveillance interval is adequate for it
Tissue diagnosis with staging, followed by lobectomy if clinical stage I disease is confirmed
Empiric radiotherapy to the nodule without a biopsy or nodal sampling
Wedge resection chosen over lobectomy for every nodule of this size
items.explanation: A spiculated, PET-avid nodule in a smoker is highly suspicious for cancer. Confirming the diagnosis and the nodal status is followed by anatomic lobectomy with nodal sampling, which gives better local control than wedge resection for operable stage I disease. Watchful waiting delays treatment of a likely malignancy. Radiotherapy without tissue is not appropriate when the patient can undergo resection.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has a three-week history of fever and right chest pain. Pleural fluid has a pH of 6.9, glucose of 30 mg/dL, and Gram-positive cocci on stain. Chest tube drainage provides only partial relief. What should be done next?
options: Rely on antibiotics alone for six weeks without drainage, since the organism is susceptible to them
Repeat thoracentesis weekly and watch the pH
Insert a larger chest tube and discharge him home
Add intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy or proceed to thoracoscopic decortication
items.explanation: Low pH and glucose with organisms define a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema, which needs drainage and antibiotics. When loculations limit drainage, intrapleural fibrinolytics or video-assisted decortication releases the cavity. Antibiotics alone cannot sterilize an undrained collection. Weekly aspirations leave loculations in place. A larger tube sometimes helps but does not break up septations, and sending him home is unsafe.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has lower abdominal pain, vaginal spotting, and amenorrhea for seven weeks. Blood pressure is 88/50 mm Hg and heart rate is 124 beats per minute. Free fluid is seen in the pelvis and Morison pouch, and the pregnancy test is positive. What is the next step?
options: Methotrexate therapy and repeat hormone levels in two days
Admit for serial beta hCG without intervention
Emergency operation for a ruptured ectopic pregnancy after resuscitation begins
Dilation and curettage to confirm the location
items.explanation: Hypotension, tachycardia, and free pelvic and upper abdominal fluid with a positive pregnancy test indicate ruptured ectopic pregnancy, which needs immediate surgery, usually laparoscopic salpingectomy in stable patients or laparotomy when unstable, with resuscitation in parallel. Methotrexate is for stable, unruptured cases. Serial testing delays treatment, and curettage does not control bleeding. Resuscitation and surgery run together.

items.stem: Three days after esophagectomy, a 64-year-old man has chest tube output of 1.5 liters of milky fluid daily. Pleural fluid triglycerides are high. He is stable. After initial dietary modification fails, which next step is most appropriate?
options: Thoracic duct ligation by thoracoscopy or thoracotomy, or percutaneous duct embolization
Continue high-fat feeding and expect spontaneous resolution
Remove the chest tube because the fluid is sterile and the patient is clinically stable after the dietary change
Perform a total gastrectomy to reduce lymph flow
items.explanation: Chylothorax after esophagectomy is confirmed by pleural triglycerides above 110 mg/dL, and high output beyond about a liter daily despite diet and bowel rest predicts failure of conservative care. Duct ligation or embolization is then indicated to avoid malnutrition and immune loss. High-fat feeding raises chyle flow. Removing the tube leaves a growing effusion, and gastrectomy does not address the duct.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 20 weeks of gestation has two days of right-sided abdominal pain, nausea, and a white count of 15,000. Ultrasound is nondiagnostic. What is the best next step?
options: Withhold any imaging and wait until delivery
Computed tomography with oral contrast as the first test regardless of availability of other options
Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen, then appendectomy if appendicitis is confirmed
Discharge on antibiotics for presumed pyelonephritis
items.explanation: Appendicitis is the most common nonobstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy, and delay raises maternal and fetal risk from perforation. After a nondiagnostic ultrasound, MRI avoids radiation and is preferred, and surgery should not be postponed for pregnancy. Waiting until delivery risks rupture. CT is used only when MRI is unavailable. Treating empirically for pyelonephritis would miss the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 9-month-old girl has episodic inconsolable crying with drawing up of the legs, then vomiting, and passes a stool resembling red currant jelly. She is stable and has no peritonitis. Ultrasound shows a target sign. What is the first-line treatment?
options: Emergency laparotomy for all cases
Oral antibiotics with outpatient observation
Nasogastric decompression and waiting for spontaneous resolution
Air or contrast enema reduction with surgical backup
items.explanation: Intussusception in a stable child without peritonitis or perforation is treated by pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction, which is highly successful, with a surgeon available in case of failure. Laparotomy is for peritonitis, perforation, or failed reduction. Antibiotics and observation do not release the telescoped bowel, and decompression alone risks ischemia from continued compression. Surgeon backup is kept because reduction can fail.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with lung cancer has a mediastinoscopy showing cancer in an ipsilateral lower paratracheal node. Her primary tumor is 3 cm and resectable. Which statement best reflects current management of this finding?
options: Immediate lobectomy alone gives cure in nearly all such patients and avoids the toxicity of systemic treatment
Neoadjuvant or definitive chemoradiation is generally used, since resection alone has poor survival
Observation is adequate until she develops symptoms of spread
The finding is stage I and needs no systemic treatment of any kind
items.explanation: Cancer in ipsilateral mediastinal nodes is N2 disease, stage III, and surgery alone has poor results because of micrometastatic spread. Management uses chemoradiation or induction therapy, with surgery selected for some patients, and immunotherapy is increasingly added. Calling it stage I ignores the node. Observation allows progression, and lobectomy alone does not cure most N2 patients.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has a two-month history of morning headaches, personality change, and a new focal seizure. MRI shows a single ring-enhancing lesion in the frontal lobe with surrounding edema. She has no known cancer. What is the best next step?
options: Systemic staging and neurosurgical evaluation for biopsy or resection
Begin empiric antibiotics for six weeks and recheck in two months
Lumbar puncture to obtain cerebrospinal fluid cytology
Reassurance and no treatment because seizures are controlled
items.explanation: A solitary enhancing lesion in an older adult may be a primary tumor, a metastasis, or an abscess, so staging for a primary site and neurosurgical evaluation for tissue diagnosis or resection are needed, with corticosteroids for edema. Empiric antibiotics are not justified without infection signs. Lumbar puncture is risky with mass effect and rarely diagnostic. Doing nothing leaves the lesion untreated.

items.stem: A 63-year-old postmenopausal woman has abdominal distension and early satiety. Imaging shows a 12 cm complex pelvic mass with solid components, ascites, and omental caking. CA-125 is markedly elevated. What is the best treatment strategy?
options: Drainage of ascites and observation without surgery, reserving chemotherapy for later symptomatic relapse of disease
Surgical staging and cytoreduction aiming for no visible residual disease, with platinum-based chemotherapy
Needle aspiration of the mass to confirm cysts
Pelvic radiation as the sole treatment
items.explanation: Advanced epithelial ovarian cancer is treated with maximal cytoreduction, because the amount of residual disease strongly predicts survival, combined with platinum-based chemotherapy. Drainage of ascites relieves symptoms only. Aspiration of a malignant mass risks spillage and does not treat. Pelvic radiation has no role as sole treatment of disease spread throughout the peritoneal cavity. Complete clearance of visible tumor is the aim.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man wakes with sudden severe right scrotal pain and vomiting. The right testis is high-riding, transversely lying, and tender, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Scrotal ultrasound first, with surgery only if Doppler flow is absent after hours of observation
Oral antibiotics for presumed epididymitis with follow-up in a week
Manual detorsion followed by discharge without surgery
Immediate surgical exploration with detorsion and fixation of both testes
items.explanation: The picture is classic torsion, a surgical emergency in which salvage falls steeply after about six hours. Exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy is performed without waiting for imaging when suspicion is high. Antibiotics are for epididymitis and delay treatment. Manual detorsion may help temporarily but surgery with fixation of both testes is still required.

items.stem: A 20-year-old tall, thin man develops sudden left chest pain and breathlessness at rest. He is hemodynamically stable, oxygen saturation is 95 percent, and chest radiography shows a 4 cm apical air rim. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Small-bore catheter aspiration or drainage with observation
Immediate left thoracotomy with pleural stripping
Needle decompression in the second intercostal space only
Discharge with no imaging follow-up because the pneumothorax is small
items.explanation: A large primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a stable patient is managed by simple aspiration or a small catheter, with oxygen and observation. Surgery is for recurrence, persistent air leak, or bilateral disease. Needle decompression is for tension physiology, which is absent here. Sending him home without follow-up ignores a rim over 2 cm, which is not small and carries risk of progression.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has a pedestrian injury with flank hematuria. He is hemodynamically stable. CT shows a deep renal laceration with a small perinephric hematoma and no urine extravasation or devascularization. What is the best management?
options: Immediate nephrectomy for a deep laceration
Surgical exploration through a midline laparotomy to repair the laceration directly in this stable patient
Nonoperative management with bed rest, monitoring, and serial hemoglobin checks
Discharge home with no monitoring
items.explanation: Most blunt renal injuries in stable patients, including many high-grade ones, are managed without surgery, with close observation and serial hemoglobin. Exploration is for hemodynamic instability, expanding retroperitoneal hematoma, or avulsion of the pedicle. Nephrectomy would sacrifice a kidney that can usually be saved. Discharge without monitoring risks missed delayed bleeding. Close monitoring still catches delayed bleeding early.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has headaches, galactorrhea, and amenorrhea. MRI shows a 7 mm pituitary mass, and the serum prolactin is 120 ng/mL with normal vision. What is the best initial treatment?
options: Transsphenoidal surgery as first-line therapy
A dopamine agonist such as cabergoline
Pituitary radiation as first-line therapy
Observation without treatment because the mass is small
items.explanation: A prolactinoma presents with galactorrhea and amenorrhea in women, and dopamine agonists normalize prolactin and shrink the tumor in most patients, making medical therapy first line even for larger tumors. Surgery is for intolerance or resistance, or when the drug fails to protect vision. Radiation is a slow, later option. Observation is inappropriate in a symptomatic patient with infertility and bone loss risk.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has postcoital bleeding. A 3 cm exophytic cervical lesion extends to the upper vagina but not to the pelvic wall, and biopsy shows squamous carcinoma. Which treatment is standard for this stage?
options: Simple hysterectomy alone
Cone biopsy with observation
Concurrent platinum-based chemotherapy and pelvic radiation
Radical hysterectomy alone for all patients with vaginal extension
items.explanation: Locally advanced cervical cancer that extends beyond the cervix to the upper vagina is treated by concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiation, which improves survival over radiation alone. Simple hysterectomy and cone biopsy are for very early or preinvasive disease. Radical hysterectomy is limited to early stages, and those with vaginal extension generally need chemoradiation instead. Stage decides the modality.

items.stem: A newborn has intestines outside the abdomen, with no covering membrane, to the right of an intact umbilical cord. The bowel is thickened and edematous. Compared with the other major abdominal wall defect, which is correct?
options: Gastroschisis rarely has associated chromosomal anomalies but often has intestinal atresia
Gastroschisis is covered by a sac and carries a high risk of trisomy and associated cardiac and renal anomalies
Omphalocele is to the right of the cord with no covering
Gastroschisis is usually associated with cardiac and renal anomalies
items.explanation: Gastroschisis is a defect to the right of an intact cord with exposed, inflamed bowel and no sac, and it is seldom linked to chromosomal syndromes, though bowel atresia occurs. Omphalocele has a sac, arises at the cord, and is linked to trisomies and cardiac, renal, and other anomalies. The distractors reverse these features, so recognizing the covering and cord relationship is key.

items.stem: A 26-year-old man has a firm, painless, 2 cm mass in the left testis found during self-examination. Scrotal ultrasound shows a hypoechoic intratesticular mass, and tumor markers are drawn. What is the correct approach to the primary tumor?
options: Transscrotal biopsy to confirm the diagnosis first
Observation with repeat ultrasound in three months
Partial orchiectomy through a scrotal incision
Radical inguinal orchiectomy with high ligation of the cord
items.explanation: A solid intratesticular mass is considered cancer and is treated by radical inguinal orchiectomy, ligating the cord at the internal ring so that lymphatic drainage to the retroperitoneum is not altered. A scrotal approach or biopsy risks violating a different lymphatic pathway to the inguinal nodes. Observation delays treatment, and partial orchiectomy is considered only in selected circumstances, not as routine management.
